_comment: Shared test matrix for the cross-language agreement test. Read by BOTH dashboard/lib/media-limits.test.ts and worker/tests/test_media_limits_agreement.py — a case added here is automatically covered on both sides. Every asset/expect pair below was verified against worker/media_limits.py's actual behavior against dashboard/media-limits.json as committed by Task 1; do not hand-edit an `expect` without re-checking it runs.
_coverage_note: max_width IS now exercised (Instagram feed.video and story.video, Task 3, both cap width at 1920) — see the instagram/feed video and instagram/story video too_large-by-width cases below. max_height is still NOT exercised anywhere below — no entry in dashboard/media-limits.json defines it, and inventing one just to test against would be a guessed limit, which this design forbids. instagram.feed.image deliberately does NOT define min_width/max_width at all (Meta auto-scales out-of-range width instead of refusing it, per that entry's note), so it has no width case here either — that is intentional, not a gap to fill. Task 6 (TikTok/Telegram/Discord/Threads) added threads.feed.image (max_bytes + a one-sided max_aspect only — Threads' own docs state no min_aspect, unlike Instagram's), telegram.feed.image (max_bytes), and a discord.feed.image case proving a huge byte_size still passes because that entry's max_bytes is deliberately null (varies by Nitro/boost — see its note). None of the three define width/height/duration bounds at all, so max_height stays unexercised for the same reason as before: no entry anywhere defines it. TikTok defines nothing in media-limits.json (its limits are per-creator and fetched at runtime via the creator-info endpoint, not a static fact — see reference.md), so it has no cases here either. A case was added proving threads.feed.image's absent min_aspect never refuses a tall/narrow image (400x4000) — see that case's own note for why it's not redundant with the max_aspect boundary cases. severity:'warn' is STILL not exercised anywhere below, and cannot be with the current data: discord.feed.image is the only entry with a `varies` note, and its max_bytes is null, so worker/media_limits.py's check() (and its TypeScript twin) never reach the comparison that would append a Violation for it in the first place — severity is computed but nothing ever carries it out. This is deliberate, not a gap: Discord's real limit depends on the poster's Nitro tier and the destination server's Boost Tier, neither of which this install can read at runtime, so no number is honest enough to enforce even as a warning (see that entry's note in media-limits.json). The warn branch would only become exercisable if some future entry combined a real numeric bound WITH a varies note — i.e. a limit that is honest as a floor/ceiling for everyone but known to be looser for some accounts. No such entry exists yet. Separately: no test anywhere would fail if the `supportsImages(platform)` filter were dropped from anyDestinationAccepts's image branch (media-limits.ts) — that filter's own union with the video branch is unconditionally true today regardless of whether it fires. Facebook has `supportsImages: true` in dashboard/lib/platforms.ts but NO image entry anywhere under facebook in media-limits.json, so checkMedia already returns [] (no violations) for it with or without the filter; Discord's image entry has max_bytes: null (see the `varies` case above), so it also passes unconditionally either way. This would only become an observable branch if some platform combined `supportsImages: false` with an image entry that WOULD refuse a given asset — i.e. a real limit recorded for a platform whose image path is deliberately unsupported. No such combination exists yet, and this is deliberately not tested against a hypothetical one. FINDING 1 (final review): `check()`/`checkMedia()` now skip the aspect-ratio and byte-size checks when the destination actually receives a conformed derivative (assets.publish_path) rather than the untouched original — conformance guarantees the sent file already satisfies both, by construction. Covered by six cases added under instagram/feed (the iPhone-portrait regression pin at 1179x2556 plus its un-conformed control, a conform_mode-only byte-size case, and a video-side byte-size case), one under facebook/feed video (proving the skip does NOT apply to a non-conform-requiring surface even when publish_path happens to be set), and one under instagram/story (proving the skip does NOT apply to Story either, even with publish_path set — _resolve_rel never reads the feed-shaped derivative there). min/max width/height checks are deliberately UNAFFECTED by this — no case here exercises a conform-skip on those, because no entry in media-limits.json defines width bounds for an image, and a video's stored width/height already describe the derivative by the time it reaches this check (the upload route overwrites them on conversion), so there was never a mismatch to skip. FINDING 5 (final review): the agreement test on both sides now compares `severity` alongside `kind` for every case here, not `kind` alone — before this, the varies -> "warn" mapping could be reverted in ONE language with a fully green suite. `message` is deliberately still NOT compared cross-language and never will be from this file alone: Python formats numbers with Python's `:g` float format, TypeScript with plain division (`entry.max_duration_ms / 1000`), which happen to agree for every value recorded in media-limits.json today (all are exact multiples of 1000ms, so `:g` never has anything to trim) but are not guaranteed to for some future value — e.g. a hypothetical 1500ms bound would render as "1.5s" in both today, but the two formatters are not the same code and could diverge on a value neither language has been asked to render yet. This is a known, accepted gap, not an oversight: message text is UI copy, not a fact either side can be wrong about the way a boundary number can, so cross-language equality would mostly be pinning incidental formatting rather than testing anything real.

cases._note: exactly the minimum size (540x960) AND exactly the minimum aspect ratio at once: 540*16 == 960*9 == 8640, so this is precisely 9:16. One case pins BOTH inclusive edges — min_width/min_height (too_small would fire below this) and min_aspect (wrong_aspect would fire below this). Don't 'simplify' the dimensions later without noticing it stops covering both. Restored after facebook-reel-spec.test.ts (Facebook-Reels-only, pre-Task-4) was deleted when Task 4 generalized the picker/worker to the shared matrix — that file's 'exactly the minimum resolution (540x960) is NOT disabled' case had no equivalent here until now.

ratio 400:1200 = 1:3 = 0.333, outside [9/16, 16/9] = [0.5625, 1.778] on the low side, AND width 400 < min_width 540 — deliberately trips too_small AND wrong_aspect together. Don't round to nicer numbers without re-checking both still fire.
exactly AT max_bytes — bounds are inclusive everywhere; a careless `>=` would wrongly refuse this
unknown byte_size must never refuse, same as unknown duration/width/height

FINDING 1 (conform-skip mechanism, negative case): facebook/feed video is NOT conform-requiring — feed_video_is_constrained is false because the /videos edge accepts any aspect ratio, so _resolve_rel (worker/publisher.py) prefers the untouched original for this surface even when a conformed derivative exists (e.g. because the same asset ALSO targets Instagram Reels, which IS conform-requiring). publish_path/conform_mode being set on the row must NOT suppress this byte-size check the way it would for a conform-requiring surface — same byte_size as the too_large case just above, still refused.
max_width boundary — exactly 1920px, aspect 1920:1080=1.778 well within [0.01,10]
ratio 1000:99 ≈ 10.10, just above the 10 ceiling; width 1000 stays under max_width so this isolates wrong_aspect alone

FINDING 1 regression pin — the reported bug, verbatim: an ordinary iPhone portrait photo (1179x2556, ratio ~0.461) fails instagram.feed.image's aspect range (min_aspect 4:5=0.8) on its OWN dimensions, but this asset already has a conformed derivative (publish_path set, built at upload time by dashboard/lib/conform.ts). The FILE Meta actually receives is the cropped derivative, which is in-range by construction — so this must NOT be wrong_aspect. Before the fix, checkMedia/check() applied the aspect check to the original's width/height regardless, and this case would have wrongly disabled the Instagram Feed chip for the owner's most common content.

Control for the case above: the SAME portrait photo, but with no publish_path/conform_mode at all — the pre-conform state (or a row predating the conform pipeline, or a conform that failed and fell back to null — see upload/route.ts's catch block). Without a conformed derivative, the original really would be sent as-is, so this must still refuse. Proves the fix is conditional on actually having a derivative, not a blanket 'never check aspect' regression.

FINDING 1, byte-size side, and proves conform_mode ALONE (no publish_path) also counts as 'has a conformed derivative' per the fix's OR condition. Aspect is already in-range (1000x1000 = 1:1, within 0.8..1.91) so this isolates the byte-size skip alone: 9MB is over instagram.feed.image's 8MB cap, but conform.ts's encodeUnderLimit guarantees the actually-sent file is under it by construction.

Same conform-skip mechanism, VIDEO side: instagram/feed IS conform-requiring (needs_conformed_media=true, feed_video_is_constrained=true), so a huge byte_size on an asset that already has a conformed derivative must not refuse on byte size either — the derivative, not this row's byte_size, is what's actually sent. (Finding 3's separate fix keeps a converted video's byte_size accurate, so this exact combination — correct width/height but a wildly wrong byte_size — shouldn't occur in practice after that fix; this case pins the check() mechanism itself, independent of Finding 3.)
max_duration_ms boundary — exactly 60s, the owner's original bug: this is the number that was missing entirely before this task
ratio 1001:100 = 10.01, just above the 10 ceiling; width 1001 stays under max_width so this isolates wrong_aspect alone
instagram.story.image max_bytes boundary — exactly 8MB. No aspect case here: that entry deliberately omits min_aspect/max_aspect (see its note).

FINDING 1, the subtle carve-out: instagram/story is EXCLUDED from 'receives the conformed derivative' even though THIS asset has a publish_path (e.g. the same asset was also uploaded/used as a Feed image, or content-hash dedup handed back a row that already has one). worker/publisher.py's _resolve_rel always prefers a Story's own 9:16 canvas or the untouched original over the feed-shaped derivative at publish_path for the story surface — it never even asks _needs_conformed. So the byte-size check must still run against this asset's own byte_size here. Must NOT be silently skipped just because publish_path happens to be set — the regression this case guards is exactly that over-broad simplification (treating ANY publish_path as 'this surface is covered').
max_aspect boundary — exactly 10:1, the only bound the page states (no min_aspect exists on this entry, see its note)

threads.feed.image is the FIRST entry in this file to record a max_aspect with NO min_aspect. This case proves the absent min_aspect never refuses: 400x4000 is ratio 0.1, far below where a min_aspect would sit if one existed (Instagram's comparable floors are 0.8 and 0.01) — a genuinely tall/narrow image, not just 'not extremely wide'. Do not delete this as redundant with the 10:1 cases above: those only prove the UPPER bound works, this proves the MISSING lower bound doesn't silently start refusing after a refactor.
telegram.feed.image max_bytes boundary — exactly 10MB (10*1024*1024), the direct-upload photo figure

discord.feed.image sets max_bytes to null (varies by Nitro tier/server boost — see that entry's note), so even a huge byte_size must never refuse. This is the case the varies design exists to prove: an unenforceable limit must degrade to 'never blocks', not 'guess and sometimes wrongly refuse'.
